commands.desc: Sign in with your Google account
commands.tooltip: Opens a browser window to authenticate gcloud with your Google account, storing OAuth credentials locally in ~/.config/gcloud. Required once per machine before most gcloud commands work. Use gcloud auth list to see which accounts are active, and gcloud auth revoke to sign out.

commands.desc: Sign in without automatically opening a browser
commands.tooltip: Prints a verification URL and code to paste into a browser on any device, handy for headless servers or SSH sessions with no display. After authorizing in the browser, paste the returned code back into the terminal. Works like plain gcloud auth login but never tries to launch a local browser.

commands.desc: Set up Application Default Credentials
commands.tooltip: Stores credentials that code libraries (Python, Node, Go SDKs) pick up automatically, separate from the gcloud CLI's own login. Use it when a local script needs to call Google APIs without embedding a service account key. The credentials land in ~/.config/gcloud/application_default_credentials.json and are removed with gcloud auth application-default revoke.

commands.desc: Show accounts with active credentials
commands.tooltip: Prints every Google account that has stored gcloud credentials, marking the currently active one with an asterisk. Use gcloud auth login to add accounts and gcloud config set account to switch between them. Add --filter=status:ACTIVE to hide expired credentials.

commands.desc: Revoke stored credentials for an account
commands.tooltip: Deletes the locally saved OAuth credentials for the given account, forcing the next gcloud auth login to re-authenticate. Useful when an account should no longer be usable from this machine or its credentials look compromised. Run gcloud auth revoke --all to clear every saved account at once.

commands.desc: Activate a service account from a key file
commands.tooltip: Makes gcloud act as a service account instead of a personal login, reading its private key from a JSON file downloaded from IAM. Service accounts are non-human identities meant for automation and CI pipelines. Generate the key file with gcloud iam service-accounts keys create, then confirm the switch with gcloud auth list.

commands.desc: Configure Docker to push to Google registries
commands.tooltip: Registers gcloud as a credential helper so docker push and docker pull work against gcr.io, us.gcr.io and similar registries using your current gcloud login. Run it once after installing Docker or after re-authenticating. Afterwards you can push images with docker push gcr.io/my-project-123456/web-app:v1.

commands.desc: Set the default project for all commands
commands.tooltip: Points every gcloud command at the given project ID so you rarely need to pass --project. A project is the top-level container that holds all your Google Cloud resources and bills their usage. Confirm the value with gcloud config get-value project or override per command with --project.

commands.desc: Show all active gcloud configuration settings
commands.tooltip: Prints the current project, account, compute region and zone plus any other properties set in the active configuration. Each property can be overridden per command with flags like --project or --region. Run gcloud config list --all to include defaults that are not explicitly set.

commands.desc: Set the default Compute Engine region
commands.tooltip: Makes us-central1 the region gcloud uses for new resources when you omit --region, saving typing and preventing mistakes. A region is a geographic area, here Iowa, that contains several zones. Related: gcloud config set compute/zone pins a specific zone inside the region.

commands.desc: Set the default Compute Engine zone
commands.tooltip: Pins gcloud to one zone, us-central1-a, an availability zone in Iowa, so instance commands work without repeating --zone. Choose a zone close to your users and spread redundant instances across zones. See gcloud compute zones list for all options.

commands.desc: Print the currently configured project ID
commands.tooltip: Outputs just the project ID string, making it easy to embed in scripts or verify which project you are about to touch. Run it before destructive commands to confirm you are working in the right project. Related: gcloud config list shows every setting at once.

commands.desc: Create a named gcloud configuration profile
commands.tooltip: Saves a fresh, empty configuration called work that can hold its own project, account and region settings. Switch between profiles with gcloud config configurations activate to move between work and personal projects without re-editing properties. List profiles with gcloud config configurations list.

commands.desc: Switch to a named gcloud configuration
commands.tooltip: Makes the work configuration active so its project, account and region defaults apply to all commands. Each configuration is an independent set of settings, ideal for keeping separate Google accounts or projects isolated. Create profiles first with gcloud config configurations create.

commands.desc: Show SDK installation and environment details
commands.tooltip: Prints where gcloud is installed, its version, the active account and project, plus environment variables like CLOUDSDK_CONFIG that alter its behaviour. Useful when debugging why gcloud behaves unexpectedly on a machine. A healthy install also reports the bundled Python interpreter and proxy settings.

commands.desc: Update gcloud and all components to the latest version
commands.tooltip: Downloads and installs newer versions of the gcloud CLI and its optional components such as kubectl and the alpha/beta command groups. Requires write access to the SDK directory, so run with sudo if gcloud lives under /usr/lib. Check what is installed first with gcloud components list.

commands.desc: List installed and available gcloud components
commands.tooltip: Shows every SDK component with its current version, state (Installed, Update Available, Not Installed) and size. Use it to see which optional tools like kubectl or gke-gcloud-auth-plugin are present. Install or remove components with gcloud components install and gcloud components remove.

commands.desc: Show gcloud version and component versions
commands.tooltip: Prints the SDK version number plus the versions of each installed component, which is the first thing support asks for when troubleshooting. Also reports the bundled Python version gcloud relies on. Compare against the current release with gcloud components update.

commands.desc: Run the first-time gcloud setup wizard
commands.tooltip: Interactive walkthrough that authenticates your Google account, picks a default project and sets the compute region and zone in one go. The fastest way to configure a fresh machine, though each step can be done individually with gcloud auth login and gcloud config set. It can also create a brand new project for you.

commands.desc: List all projects you can access
commands.tooltip: Prints every Google Cloud project visible to your account with its ID, name and project number. Project IDs are globally unique and appear in commands and URLs, while names are just human-friendly labels. Filter with --filter=name:my or reshape the table with --format.

commands.desc: Create a new Google Cloud project
commands.tooltip: Provisions a brand new project with the given ID, which must be globally unique across all of Google Cloud and follow DNS-style lowercase naming. The --name flag sets the friendly label shown in the console. New projects start empty, so enable the APIs you need with gcloud services enable.

commands.desc: Show details for a single project
commands.tooltip: Prints metadata for one project including its ID, number, name and the resource parent (an organization or folder). Useful in scripts to fetch the project number, which some IAM policies require. Related: gcloud projects list shows all projects at once.

commands.desc: Delete a project and all its resources
commands.tooltip: Permanently removes the project and every resource inside it, including VMs, buckets, databases and billing history, with no trash bin. Google keeps the project ID locked for 30 days after deletion, so it cannot be reused immediately. Run gcloud projects list first to be certain you are deleting the right project.

commands.desc: Enable an API for the current project
commands.tooltip: Turns on a Google Cloud service, here Compute Engine, for the active project, which is required before you can create its resources. API names follow the pattern service.googleapis.com, browseable with gcloud services list --available. Enabling compute.googleapis.com unlocks commands like gcloud compute instances create.

commands.desc: List APIs currently enabled for the project
commands.tooltip: Shows every API active in the current project, each identified by its service name like compute.googleapis.com. Use it to confirm a service is on before calling its commands, since disabled APIs return permission errors. Browse everything Google offers with gcloud services list --available.

commands.desc: Disable an API for the current project
commands.tooltip: Switches off a Google Cloud service so its resources can no longer be created or managed, which can break running workloads that depend on it. Only disable services you are sure nothing uses. Re-enable anytime with gcloud services enable.

commands.desc: List all VM instances in the project
commands.tooltip: Prints every Compute Engine virtual machine across all zones with its name, zone, machine type, internal and external IPs and status. Add --filter=status:RUNNING to see only running VMs, or --format='table(name,zone,status)' to trim columns. Instances that are stopped but not deleted still appear in this list.

commands.cmd: gcloud compute instances create web-server --zone us-central1-a --machine-type e2-micro
commands.desc: Create a minimal VM instance
commands.tooltip: Provisions a virtual machine named web-server in zone us-central1-a using the cheap e2-micro shared-core machine type. Without --image-family it defaults to a recent Debian image. Add --tags http-server now so firewall rules can target this VM later.

commands.cmd: gcloud compute instances create db-server --zone us-central1-a --machine-type e2-standard-2 --image-family ubuntu-2404-lts --image-project ubuntu-os-cloud
commands.desc: Create an Ubuntu VM with more vCPUs and RAM
commands.tooltip: Builds a db-server VM with 2 vCPUs and 8 GB RAM running Ubuntu 24.04 LTS, selected via --image-family and --image-project ubuntu-os-cloud. The e2-standard-2 tier suits small databases and general workloads. See gcloud compute images list for other families like debian-12 or rocky-linux-9.

commands.cmd: gcloud compute instances describe web-server --zone us-central1-a
commands.desc: Show detailed information about a VM
commands.tooltip: Prints a full description of one instance: machine type, disks, network interfaces, tags, metadata and scheduling policy. Add --format='value(networkInterfaces[0].accessConfigs[0].natIP)' to extract just the external IP. Related: gcloud compute instances list for a compact table.

commands.cmd: gcloud compute instances start web-server --zone us-central1-a
commands.desc: Start a stopped VM instance
commands.tooltip: Boots a previously stopped instance back up, restoring its disks and IP configuration. Billing for the instance only runs while it is in the RUNNING state. Pair with gcloud compute instances stop for simple on/off cost control.

commands.cmd: gcloud compute instances stop web-server --zone us-central1-a
commands.desc: Stop a running VM instance
commands.tooltip: Shuts the VM down cleanly so you stop paying for compute time, while persistent disks and static IPs are kept and billed separately. The instance remains in the project and can be restarted with gcloud compute instances start. Data on standard persistent disks survives a stop.

commands.cmd: gcloud compute instances delete web-server --zone us-central1-a
commands.desc: Delete a VM instance permanently
commands.tooltip: Removes the instance and, by default, its attached boot disk, destroying all data on it with no recovery. Add --keep-disks=boot to preserve the disk or --delete-disks=all to also wipe extra data disks. Snapshot important disks first with gcloud compute disks snapshot.

commands.desc: Open an SSH session to a VM instance
commands.tooltip: Connects to the instance over SSH using your Google account, generating and uploading an SSH key on first use so no manual key setup is needed. Requires the instance to have a public IP or IAP tunnel access. Exit with Ctrl-D, or run a single command instead with the --command flag.

commands.desc: Run one command on a VM over SSH
commands.tooltip: Executes the quoted command on the instance and prints the output, then closes the connection, which makes it perfect for scripts and one-off checks. Chain several steps with && inside the quotes. Interactive sessions without --command are covered by plain gcloud compute ssh.

commands.cmd: gcloud compute scp deploy.sh web-server:/home/alex/ --zone us-central1-a
commands.desc: Copy a file to a VM instance
commands.tooltip: Securely copies a local file to the instance using the same key handling as gcloud compute ssh, so no separate scp setup is needed. The destination takes the form USER@INSTANCE:REMOTE_PATH, where /home/alex/ is the home of the connecting user. Copy whole directories by adding --recurse.

commands.cmd: gcloud compute scp --recurse build/ web-server:/home/alex/app/ --zone us-central1-a
commands.desc: Copy a directory tree to a VM recursively
commands.tooltip: Uploads the entire build/ folder and all its contents into /home/alex/app/ on the instance. Without --recurse, scp only copies files at the top level and skips subdirectories. Reverse the argument order, remote first, to download files from the VM.

commands.desc: List reserved static external IP addresses
commands.tooltip: Shows every reserved static IP with its name, regional or global scope, address and status (RESERVED or IN_USE). Static IPs stay assigned to your project even when no VM uses them, and they keep billing while reserved. Reserve a new one with gcloud compute addresses reserve.

commands.cmd: gcloud compute addresses reserve web-ip --region us-central1
commands.desc: Reserve a static external IP address
commands.tooltip: Claims a permanent public IPv4 address named web-ip in the us-central1 region so it survives VM restarts and deletions. Regional addresses attach to instances in that region, while global ones (--global) are used by load balancers. You pay for reserved addresses even while unused, so release them with gcloud compute addresses delete when done.

commands.cmd: gcloud compute addresses delete web-ip --region us-central1
commands.desc: Release a reserved static IP address
commands.tooltip: Returns the reserved IP to Google's pool, permanently losing that address, which can break DNS records or firewall allowlists pointing at it. You stop paying the reservation fee once released. Check what references the address first with gcloud compute addresses list.

commands.desc: List VPC firewall rules
commands.tooltip: Prints all firewall rules in the project with their direction, allowed protocols and ports, target tags, source ranges and enforcement status. Rules are stateful and apply at the network level, not inside the instance OS. See gcloud compute firewall-rules describe for the full JSON of one rule.

commands.cmd: gcloud compute firewall-rules create allow-http --allow tcp:80,tcp:443 --target-tags http-server
commands.desc: Create a firewall rule allowing web traffic
commands.tooltip: Opens inbound TCP ports 80 and 443 for every VM carrying the http-server network tag, which you set with --tags when creating instances. Without --target-tags the rule applies to all instances in the network, so tags keep exposure narrow. Delete it with gcloud compute firewall-rules delete, and remember the OS-level firewall must also permit the port.

commands.desc: Delete a firewall rule
commands.tooltip: Permanently removes the rule, immediately blocking whatever traffic it allowed, which can take down websites or APIs that depended on it. Check which instances rely on the rule with gcloud compute firewall-rules describe first. Recreate it later with gcloud compute firewall-rules create.

commands.desc: List persistent disks in the project
commands.tooltip: Shows every persistent disk with its zone, size, type (pd-standard, pd-balanced, pd-ssd) and the instance it is attached to, if any. Disks exist independently of VMs, so they survive instance deletion unless you choose to delete them. Filter by zone with --filter=zone:us-central1-a.

commands.cmd: gcloud compute disks snapshot web-disk --snapshot-names web-disk-snap-20260801 --zone us-central1-a
commands.desc: Snapshot a persistent disk for backup
commands.tooltip: Captures a point-in-time backup of the web-disk disk named web-disk-snap-20260801, stored redundantly in Cloud Storage. Snapshots are incremental, so repeated snapshots only cost the changed data. Restore one by creating a new disk with --source-snapshot or use it to clone the disk into another zone.

commands.cmd: gcloud compute disks delete data-disk --zone us-central1-a
commands.desc: Delete a persistent disk
commands.tooltip: Permanently erases the disk and all data on it, which fails if the disk is still attached to a running instance unless you add --force. Take a snapshot with gcloud compute disks snapshot before deleting anything important. Deleting a disk frees its storage cost but removes all recovery options.

commands.desc: List all disk snapshots
commands.tooltip: Prints every snapshot in the project with its source disk, size and creation time. Snapshots are the standard backup mechanism for Compute Engine disks and can restore data to any zone. Create them with gcloud compute disks snapshot.

commands.desc: List available public VM images
commands.tooltip: Shows the OS images you can boot VMs from, including Debian, Ubuntu, Rocky Linux and Windows families, with their projects and architectures. Use values from the IMAGE column with --image and --image-project when creating instances. Add --filter=family:ubuntu-2404 to narrow the list.

commands.desc: List Compute Engine regions and statuses
commands.tooltip: Prints every region where you can create resources, like us-central1 (Iowa) and europe-west1 (Belgium), along with whether each is UP. Each region contains several zones for distributing workloads. Zones inside a region are listed by gcloud compute zones list.

commands.desc: List Cloud Storage buckets in the project
commands.tooltip: Prints the gs:// URLs of every bucket in your default project. Buckets are the top-level containers for objects, the files of Cloud Storage, and their names must be globally unique. Drill into a bucket's contents with gsutil ls gs://bucket-name/.

commands.desc: List objects inside a bucket
commands.tooltip: Shows all objects, the files of Cloud Storage, stored at the top level of my-bucket. Add -r to recurse into prefixes or a wildcard like gs://my-bucket/*.log to filter by name. Object paths look like folders but are flat keys in Cloud Storage.

commands.desc: List objects with size and timestamps
commands.tooltip: Adds the object size in bytes, creation time and storage class to each listed entry, handy for spotting large files. Combine with -r to scan the whole bucket recursively. For total bucket size, use gsutil du -sh gs://my-bucket/.

commands.desc: Upload a file to a bucket
commands.tooltip: Copies the local file report.pdf into my-bucket, where it becomes an object addressable at gs://my-bucket/report.pdf. The file keeps its base name unless you give a different destination name. Copy whole directories with the -r flag, or use -m for parallel speed on many files.

commands.desc: Download an object from a bucket
commands.tooltip: Fetches report.pdf from my-bucket into the current directory. The destination can be any local path, or another bucket to copy between buckets. Larger transfers benefit from the parallel flag: gsutil -m cp.

commands.desc: Upload a directory recursively
commands.tooltip: Copies the entire build/ directory tree, including subfolders, into the site/ prefix of the bucket. Without -r, gsutil skips directories entirely and only uploads top-level files. Folders appear as prefixes in the bucket, not real directories.

commands.desc: Upload a directory using parallel threads
commands.tooltip: Same recursive copy as plain cp -r but splits the work across multiple threads and connections, which is dramatically faster for many or large files. The -m flag must come before the subcommand, as in gsutil -m cp. Expect higher network usage, and on huge jobs occasional transient rate-limit errors.

commands.desc: Mirror a local directory to a bucket
commands.tooltip: Makes the bucket's site/ prefix exactly match the local build/ folder, uploading new and changed files and removing objects that no longer exist locally. The -d flag deletes extras in the destination, so test with -n first to preview changes. Ideal for deploying static websites.

commands.desc: Create a new Cloud Storage bucket
commands.tooltip: Makes a bucket named my-bucket in the default project and location. Bucket names must be globally unique across all of Google Cloud, lowercase, and 3-63 characters long. Set a region with -l us-central1 and a storage class with -c nearline for cheaper cold data.

commands.desc: Show total size of a bucket
commands.tooltip: Prints the combined size of all objects in my-bucket in human-readable form, useful for tracking storage costs. Add -a to include non-current object versions when versioning is on. A per-object listing is available via gsutil ls -l.

commands.desc: Delete a single object from a bucket
commands.tooltip: Permanently removes the old.log object; Cloud Storage gives no undo, though versioned buckets keep older copies accessible. Deleting the last object under a prefix makes that prefix disappear from listings. Delete entire buckets with gsutil rm -r gs://bucket-name.

commands.desc: Delete a bucket and all its contents
commands.tooltip: Recursively deletes every object in my-bucket and then the bucket itself, destroying all data with no recovery path. This is one of the most destructive commands in the glossary, so double-check the bucket name and consider enabling versioning first. Add -m to parallelize deletion of large buckets.

commands.desc: Grant a user read access to an object
commands.tooltip: Applies a legacy ACL granting the user alex@example.com read permission (R) on the object; W means write and FC full control. ACLs are the older permission model, while IAM roles are preferred for buckets and projects. Remove the grant by repeating the command with -d in place of -u.

commands.desc: Grant a user an IAM role on a bucket
commands.tooltip: Gives alex@example.com the objectViewer IAM role on my-bucket, letting them list and read objects there; common roles are objectViewer, objectAdmin and storageAdmin. IAM is the modern access-control system and is more flexible than legacy ACLs. Revoke with gsutil iam ch -d user:alex@example.com:objectViewer gs://my-bucket.

commands.desc: Enable object versioning on a bucket
commands.tooltip: Turns on versioning so overwritten and deleted objects keep a previous version, protecting against accidental data loss and enabling easy rollback. Older versions still cost storage, so pair this with a lifecycle policy to prune them. List versions with gsutil ls -a gs://my-bucket/.

commands.desc: Print an object's contents to stdout
commands.tooltip: Streams the contents of notes.txt to the terminal without downloading a file, handy for quick peeks at logs or config blobs. Larger files can be piped into less or head to page the output. Related: gsutil cp downloads the object for local use.

commands.desc: Move or rename an object in a bucket
commands.tooltip: Renames or relocates old.txt within the bucket; moving between buckets also copies across locations and deletes the source. It performs a copy plus delete under the hood, so a failure mid-way can leave both copies. Use gsutil cp then gsutil rm when you need more control.

commands.desc: Copy a file with the unified gcloud storage tool
commands.tooltip: Uploads report.pdf using the newer gcloud storage command family, which offers the same operations as gsutil with better performance and progress reporting. Flags like -r and -m are supported, and gcloud storage ls, rsync and rm cover the rest of the workflow. Prefer this on fresh projects; gsutil still works everywhere.

commands.desc: List bucket contents with gcloud storage
commands.tooltip: Prints the objects in my-bucket using the unified storage client, with cleaner formatting and faster listing than gsutil on large buckets. Add -r to recurse and -l for sizes and timestamps. This command lives inside the gcloud CLI, so no separate gsutil install is needed.

commands.desc: Sync a directory to a bucket with gcloud storage
commands.tooltip: Mirrors build/ into the site/ prefix of my-bucket, uploading changes and, with -d, deleting destination objects that are not in the source. Run with -n first to dry-run and review exactly what would change. It behaves like gsutil rsync but with faster parallel transfers.

commands.cmd: gcloud storage buckets create gs://my-bucket --location us-central1
commands.desc: Create a bucket with gcloud storage
commands.tooltip: Provisions my-bucket in the us-central1 region using the unified tool; bucket names must be globally unique across Google Cloud. Add --public-access-prevention to block accidental public exposure, or -c nearline for colder storage. Equivalent to gsutil mb.

commands.cmd: gcloud functions deploy hello-world --runtime python312 --trigger-http --allow-unauthenticated --region us-central1
commands.desc: Deploy an HTTP-triggered Cloud Function
commands.tooltip: Publishes the current directory's function as hello-world, running Python 3.12 and invoked by HTTPS requests. --allow-unauthenticated lets anyone on the internet call it, so omit it to require an identity token instead. The code must match the runtime; see gcloud functions runtimes list for supported versions.

commands.cmd: gcloud functions deploy process-uploads --runtime python312 --trigger-topic new-uploads --region us-central1
commands.desc: Deploy a Pub/Sub-triggered Cloud Function
commands.tooltip: Deploys process-uploads so it runs whenever a message lands on the new-uploads Pub/Sub topic, with the message payload passed to the function. Pub/Sub is Google's message queue service for decoupling services. Remove it with gcloud functions delete process-uploads --region us-central1.

commands.desc: List deployed Cloud Functions
commands.tooltip: Shows every function in the region with its runtime, trigger type, state and update time. Add --filter=state:ACTIVE to hide failed deployments. Function names must be unique within the region and project.

commands.desc: Show details of a Cloud Function
commands.tooltip: Prints the full configuration of hello-world: runtime, entry point, trigger, environment variables, timeout and the HTTPS trigger URL. Grab the URL from the httpsTrigger.url field to call the function. Related: gcloud functions logs read shows its runtime logs.

commands.desc: Invoke a Cloud Function with JSON payload
commands.tooltip: Sends a synchronous test request to the function with the given JSON body and returns the function's response in the terminal. Works for HTTP-triggered functions; pass the expected event shape in --data for background triggers. This is the quickest way to smoke-test a deploy.

commands.desc: Delete a Cloud Function
commands.tooltip: Permanently removes the function and its cloud resources, so any URLs or subscribers that called it start failing immediately. There is no undo, though redeploying from the same source restores it. List what exists first with gcloud functions list.

commands.cmd: gcloud functions logs read hello-world --region us-central1
commands.desc: Read recent logs from a Cloud Function
commands.tooltip: Pulls the latest log entries for hello-world, including print output, errors and invocation timestamps. Add --limit=100 to control volume or --filter=severity>=ERROR to see only failures. Logs live in Cloud Logging, queryable later with gcloud logging read.

commands.cmd: gcloud run deploy web-app --image gcr.io/my-project-123456/web-app:v1 --region us-central1 --allow-unauthenticated
commands.desc: Deploy a container to Cloud Run
commands.tooltip: Pushes the container image gcr.io/my-project-123456/web-app:v1 live as a serverless service that scales to zero when idle. --allow-unauthenticated makes the service reachable by anyone with the URL; drop it to require Google identity. Each deploy creates a new revision and shifts traffic to it.

commands.desc: List Cloud Run services
commands.tooltip: Prints every service in the region with its URL, latest revision and conditions such as Ready. Cloud Run services handle HTTP requests, while jobs (gcloud run jobs list) run batch workloads. Filter by service name with --filter=metadata.name:web.

commands.cmd: gcloud run services describe web-app --region us-central1
commands.desc: Show Cloud Run service configuration
commands.tooltip: Outputs the service's full spec as YAML: container image, CPU and memory limits, concurrency, environment variables and traffic split. The status.url field is the public endpoint. Related: gcloud run services update changes settings on a running service.

commands.cmd: gcloud run services update web-app --image gcr.io/my-project-123456/web-app:v2 --region us-central1
commands.desc: Deploy a new image to an existing service
commands.tooltip: Creates a new revision of web-app from the v2 image and routes all traffic to it, the standard way to ship an update. Revisions keep the old image available for instant rollback. Roll back with gcloud run services update-traffic --to-revisions=web-app-00001=100.

commands.cmd: gcloud run services update-traffic web-app --to-latest --region us-central1
commands.desc: Send all traffic to the latest revision
commands.tooltip: Moves 100% of requests to the most recently deployed revision, useful after testing a canary or recovering from a bad rollout. Use --to-revisions=NAME=PERCENT to split traffic between revisions deliberately. Check the current split with gcloud run services describe.

commands.cmd: gcloud run services delete web-app --region us-central1
commands.desc: Delete a Cloud Run service
commands.tooltip: Removes the service and all its revisions, taking the public URL offline permanently; container images in Artifact Registry are not deleted. There is no undo, so export the YAML first with gcloud run services describe --format=yaml if you may redeploy. Related: gcloud run jobs delete removes batch jobs.

commands.cmd: gcloud run jobs create nightly-cleanup --image gcr.io/my-project-123456/cleanup:v1 --region us-central1
commands.desc: Create a Cloud Run batch job
commands.tooltip: Defines a job named nightly-cleanup that runs the cleanup container to completion instead of serving HTTP requests. Jobs are for batch work like ETL or maintenance and can run on a schedule. Execute it with gcloud run jobs execute nightly-cleanup --region us-central1.

commands.cmd: gcloud run jobs execute nightly-cleanup --region us-central1
commands.desc: Run a Cloud Run job once
commands.tooltip: Starts a single execution of nightly-cleanup and reports the execution ID, which you can follow in Cloud Logging. The job's container runs to completion with retries per its configuration. Schedule recurring runs with Cloud Scheduler or pass --execute-now at creation time.

commands.desc: List Cloud Run jobs
commands.tooltip: Shows every job in the region with its creation time and latest execution status. Unlike services, jobs do not hold traffic; they exist to be executed on demand or by schedule. Inspect one job with gcloud run jobs describe.

commands.cmd: gcloud run jobs delete nightly-cleanup --region us-central1
commands.desc: Delete a Cloud Run job
commands.tooltip: Permanently removes the job and its execution history; any scheduled triggers referencing it will fail afterwards. Deleting a job does not delete its container image. Recreate it anytime with gcloud run jobs create.

commands.desc: Read Cloud Run logs with a filter
commands.tooltip: Queries Cloud Logging for the last 50 entries from web-app's revisions, filtering on the resource type cloud_run_revision. Filters use the Logging query language, so add AND severity>=ERROR for failures only. Stream live entries instead with gcloud logging tail.

commands.desc: Stream Cloud Run logs live
commands.tooltip: Follows new log entries from the web-app service in real time, like tail -f but for Google Cloud logs. Press Ctrl-C to stop streaming. Useful while deploying or load-testing; historical queries use gcloud logging read.

commands.desc: List Cloud SQL instances
commands.tooltip: Prints every managed database instance in the project with its database version (PostgreSQL, MySQL, SQL Server), region, tier and state. Cloud SQL is Google's fully managed relational database service. Instances in state RUNNABLE accept connections.

commands.cmd: gcloud sql instances create my-db --database-version POSTGRES_15 --tier db-f1-micro --region us-central1
commands.desc: Create a small PostgreSQL instance
commands.tooltip: Provisions a managed PostgreSQL 15 database named my-db on the free-tier-eligible db-f1-micro machine in us-central1. The instance starts empty, so create databases inside it with gcloud sql databases create. Cloud SQL handles backups, patching and replication for you.

commands.desc: Show Cloud SQL instance details
commands.tooltip: Prints the instance's connection name, IP address, SSL settings, backup configuration and machine tier as JSON. The connection name (project:region:instance) is what client libraries and gcloud sql connect use. Related: gcloud sql instances list for a compact view.

commands.desc: Open a psql session to a Cloud SQL instance
commands.tooltip: Starts an interactive PostgreSQL shell against my-db as the postgres user, using the Cloud SQL Auth Proxy under the hood so no public IP or manual SSL setup is needed. Exit with \q. If the psql client is missing, gcloud prompts to install it.

commands.desc: Delete a Cloud SQL instance
commands.tooltip: Permanently removes the instance, its databases and its automatic backups with no recovery, so export critical data first with gcloud sql export sql. Instances with deletion protection enabled refuse the operation until you disable it with gcloud sql instances patch my-db --deletion-protection=false. Verify the instance name with gcloud sql instances list before running.

commands.desc: List backups for a Cloud SQL instance
commands.tooltip: Shows every automated and on-demand backup for my-db with its ID, type, status and window. Automated backups run daily per the instance's backup configuration. Restore one with gcloud sql backups restore BACKUP_ID --restore-instance my-db.

commands.cmd: gcloud sql export sql my-db gs://my-bucket/dump.sql.gz --database appdb
commands.desc: Export a database to Cloud Storage
commands.tooltip: Dumps the appdb database from my-db into a compressed SQL file in my-bucket, a portable way to back up or migrate data. The instance's service account needs the storage.objectAdmin role on the bucket. Import the file into another instance with gcloud sql import sql.

commands.cmd: gcloud sql import sql my-db gs://my-bucket/dump.sql.gz --database appdb
commands.desc: Import a SQL dump into a database
commands.tooltip: Loads the SQL dump from the bucket into the appdb database on my-db, replacing its contents. The dump must come from a compatible engine version. Use it to restore backups or seed a fresh instance; create the dump with gcloud sql export sql.

commands.desc: List databases on a Cloud SQL instance
commands.tooltip: Prints every database inside my-db, which starts with the default postgres database on PostgreSQL instances. Create another with gcloud sql databases create appdb --instance my-db. Each database holds its own tables and users.

commands.cmd: gcloud iam service-accounts create deploy-bot --display-name "Deploy bot"
commands.desc: Create a service account
commands.tooltip: Provisions a non-human identity named deploy-bot that applications and CI pipelines use to call Google APIs without a person's login. The account gets an email like deploy-bot@my-project-123456.iam.gserviceaccount.com. Grant it roles with gcloud projects add-iam-policy-binding.

commands.desc: List service accounts in the project
commands.tooltip: Shows every service account with its email, display name and whether it is disabled. The default Compute Engine service account appears here too. Add --filter=disabled:false to see only usable accounts.

commands.cmd: gcloud iam service-accounts keys create key.json --iam-account deploy-bot@my-project-123456.iam.gserviceaccount.com
commands.desc: Create a service account key file
commands.tooltip: Generates a JSON private key for the service account and writes it to key.json, a long-lived credential anyone with the file can use. Treat key files like passwords, store them in a secret manager, and prefer Workload Identity Federation where possible. Delete unused keys with gcloud iam service-accounts keys delete.

commands.desc: List keys for a service account
commands.tooltip: Prints every key attached to deploy-bot with its ID, type and creation time, letting you spot stale or unexpected credentials. Old keys never expire by default, so audit this list periodically. Remove unused keys with gcloud iam service-accounts keys delete.

commands.desc: List IAM roles
commands.tooltip: Shows the built-in IAM roles like roles/storage.objectViewer and roles/compute.admin that control who can do what on Google Cloud resources. Custom roles created in your project appear here too. See what a role permits with gcloud iam roles describe roles/storage.objectViewer.

commands.desc: Grant an IAM role to a service account
commands.tooltip: Gives deploy-bot the storage.objectAdmin role on the whole project, letting it manage buckets and objects everywhere in my-project-123456. Members can also be users (user:email) or groups (group:email), and --condition can scope the grant further. Remove the grant with gcloud projects remove-iam-policy-binding.

commands.desc: Create a new Secret Manager secret
commands.tooltip: Creates a secret named my-api-key that will hold a value like an API key or password, replicated automatically across regions for availability. The secret starts with no versions, so add the first value with gcloud secrets versions add. Read the value later with gcloud secrets versions access.

commands.cmd: gcloud secrets versions access latest --secret my-api-key
commands.desc: Print the latest secret value
commands.tooltip: Outputs the newest version's value of my-api-key to the terminal, which is how scripts read secrets at runtime. Anyone holding the roles/secretmanager.secretAccessor role can do this, so keep output out of logs. List all versions with gcloud secrets versions list.

commands.desc: Add a new version to a secret
commands.tooltip: Stores the contents of key.txt as the newest version of my-api-key, replacing what latest points to. Old versions remain accessible by their version number, enabling instant rollback. Use --data-file=- to read the value from stdin.

commands.desc: List versions of a secret
commands.tooltip: Shows every version of my-api-key with its state (ENABLED, DISABLED, DESTROYED) and creation time. Destroy a version with gcloud secrets versions destroy to make it unrecoverable. Access a specific version by number instead of latest when you need an old value.

commands.desc: Delete a secret and all its versions
commands.tooltip: Schedules the secret for deletion with a 30-day grace period, during which it can be restored with gcloud secrets undelete. Applications reading the secret fail once deletion completes, so update them first. There is no undo after the grace period ends.

commands.desc: Build and push a container image with Cloud Build
commands.tooltip: Uploads the current directory to Cloud Build, which builds the Dockerfile into an image and pushes it to the registry as gcr.io/my-project-123456/web-app:v1. Requires Cloud Build enabled and registry auth set up via gcloud auth configure-docker. The resulting image feeds gcloud run deploy or other container-based services.

commands.desc: List Cloud Build jobs
commands.tooltip: Prints recent build submissions with their ID, status (SUCCESS, FAILURE, WORKING) and the source or tag built. Watch a specific build live with gcloud builds log BUILD_ID. Related: gcloud builds submit starts a new build.

commands.desc: Authorize GAM for a Google Workspace domain
commands.tooltip: First-time setup that opens Google's consent screen to authorize GAM with a Workspace super admin account, storing credentials in oauth2.txt inside the GAM directory. Run once per domain; afterwards GAM commands act with the admin's privileges. Check the authorized account with gam oauth info.

commands.desc: List all users in the domain
commands.tooltip: Outputs every user in the Workspace directory as CSV rows of primary email, first name, last name and status. Pipe the output to a file to build user lists, or add fields to widen the columns. Filter the set with the query option, as in gam print users query "isSuspended=False".

commands.desc: List users matching a directory query
commands.tooltip: Prints only the users satisfying the query string, here everyone not suspended. Queries use the Admin SDK syntax, so orgUnitPath='/Staff' narrows to an organizational unit and isArchived=False filters archived accounts. See gam print users for the unfiltered list.

commands.desc: Show details for one user
commands.tooltip: Displays a user's profile: name, primary email, aliases, organizational unit, recovery options, licenses and group memberships. Use it to verify changes made with gam update user. Add formatjson for a machine-readable dump.

commands.cmd: gam create user alex@example.com firstname "Alex" lastname "Rivera" password "TempPass123!"
commands.desc: Create a new Workspace user
commands.tooltip: Provisions a new account with the given email, display name and temporary password, ready to sign in immediately. Add ou '/Staff' to place the user in an organizational unit and notify email@address to mail the credentials. Force a password change at first login with changepasswordatnextlogin true.

commands.cmd: gam update user alex@example.com organization department "Engineering" primary
commands.desc: Update a user's department field
commands.tooltip: Sets the department on the user's organization entry to Engineering; the primary flag marks this organization record as the main one. Other organization attributes like title and costcenter can be set the same way. Verify with gam info user alex@example.com.

commands.cmd: gam update user alex@example.com recoveryemail alex.private@gmail.com
commands.desc: Set a user's recovery email
commands.tooltip: Assigns a backup email address used for account recovery and security alerts when the primary address is unavailable. Works the same way with recoveryphone for a phone number. Check the current value with gam info user.

commands.desc: Suspend a user account
commands.tooltip: Blocks the user from signing in while keeping the account, mailbox and Drive data intact, the standard first step in offboarding. Suspended users keep their licenses unless you remove them separately. Reinstate with gam unsuspend user alex@example.com.

commands.desc: Delete a user account
commands.tooltip: Permanently removes the account and its Workspace data; the primary email stays reserved for a short window during which a super admin can restore the account with gam undelete user. Transfer Drive and mail ownership to a colleague first with gam user alex@example.com transfer drive. There is no undo after the reservation window closes.

commands.desc: List all groups in the domain
commands.tooltip: Outputs every Google Group with its email, name, description and member counts. Add fields to widen the columns or pipe into a CSV for offline review. Drill into one group's members with gam print group-members group eng-team@example.com.

commands.desc: Show details for one group
commands.tooltip: Displays a group's settings: name, description, who can post, who can join, and its owners, managers and members. Handy before changing membership to see who is affected. Membership changes go through gam update group.

commands.cmd: gam create group eng-team@example.com name "Engineering Team" description "All engineers"
commands.desc: Create a new Google Group
commands.tooltip: Provisions a group with the given email address, display name and description, ready to receive members. Add members with gam update group eng-team@example.com add member user@example.com. The owner option can name an initial owner other than the admin.

commands.cmd: gam update group eng-team@example.com add member alex@example.com
commands.desc: Add a member to a group
commands.tooltip: Adds alex@example.com as a regular member of eng-team@example.com; use manager or owner instead of member to grant moderation powers. Members can be users, groups or external addresses. Remove someone with the remove member form of this command.

commands.cmd: gam update group eng-team@example.com remove member alex@example.com
commands.desc: Remove a member from a group
commands.tooltip: Takes alex@example.com out of eng-team@example.com, so they stop receiving the group's mail and lose access to resources shared through it. Use delete in place of remove for the same effect. Verify membership with gam info group eng-team@example.com.

commands.desc: Delete a Google Group
commands.tooltip: Permanently removes the group, its settings and membership, and the group address starts bouncing mail. There is no undo, so export members first with gam print group-members group eng-team@example.com. Recreating the group later requires a fresh setup.

commands.desc: List members of a group
commands.tooltip: Outputs every member of eng-team@example.com with their role (OWNER, MANAGER, MEMBER), type and status. Add recursive to include members of nested subgroups. This is the fastest way to audit who can reach a group's mail.

commands.cmd: gam calendar alex@example.com add event start 2026-09-01T10:00:00-07:00 end 2026-09-01T11:00:00-07:00 summary "Project kickoff"
commands.desc: Add an event to a user's calendar
commands.tooltip: Creates a one-hour event on alex@example.com's primary calendar starting at the given timestamp, with the summary as the event title. Times use ISO 8601 format with an offset like -07:00 for the timezone. Attach attendees by repeating the attendee option with each email.
